extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / literate public interested in manners, marriage, and literary criticism (early 18th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: Periodical essay-style guidance and criticism addressing social behaviour (marriage, friendship, parental duty) and literary quality (poetic diction, invocation, characterization). Written for a general educated readership of early-18th-century periodicals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral instruction by exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: A man improves more by reading the story of a person eminent for prudence and virtue than by the finest rules and precepts of morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete examples and narratives (letters, stories of real persons) to teach moral lessons rather than abstract maxims. The author presents a letter as an example and deliberately leaves readers to 'make his own use of it, without adding any reflections.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion in public marital behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Wedded couples should avoid performing extreme behaviours in public — neither perpetual smart repartee just within rules nor incessant public billing; public displays of private familiarities are improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose a mean between public quarrelling and ostentatious affection: either genuine, deep aversion or calm, noble love to prevent frequent observable fondness. Married women should not make 'nauseous Allusions to private Familiarities' before company; such behaviour causes embarrassment to bystanders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardianship and personal responsibility regarding flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: Those most exposed to impositions (raw/innocent young women) have guardians/parents responsible to advise and guard them; mature women who allow flattering attempts are blameworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent impositions by limiting opportunities for flattering conversation; parents and advisers should actively protect the naive. If grown women are prevailed upon, the fault lies with their failure to have wisdom grow with their years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critics should be modest and balanced
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics (the 'little Criticks') should show their small talents but not grow vain; each fop can find faults, but one will not 'arrive at Knowing when to praise' if vanity dominates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pride and constant fault-finding; cultivate the judgment to praise appropriately. Humility is a key trait for a good critic (the prologue lines encourage tempering criticism with praise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue enhances beauty — ideal female character
rubrics_metrics.description: The concurrence of wisdom and beauty is the highest female excellence; 'virtue makes a beautiful Woman appear more beautiful, so Beauty makes a virtuous Woman really more virtuous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present female characters (or real women held up as examples) who combine unstudied graces, modesty, good-humour, rational piety and chearful resignation; such combination elicits admiration and instructs others by example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as reasoned, constant, compassionate practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion should be 'a principle founded in reason and enlivened with hope' — strict without severity, compassionate without weakness; not showy fits of devotion or ostentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate religious behaviour by its consistence and humane tone rather than by formal observances or emotionally extravagant displays. True piety appears in steady moral action and good-humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reformation by example and gentle persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: To reform a husband's faults, silent example and easy, unrepining behaviour are more persuasive than severity or lectures; approve and second improvements as his own thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an 'artful train of management and unseen perswasions' — slowly make virtues appear as the husband's own ideas, thereby gaining lasting influence. Avoid harsh admonition; prefer subtle encouragement and approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain decency in dress to preserve conjugal affection
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglect of apparel (wrapping gowns, dirty linen, huddled economy of dress) even in private reduces conjugal regard; small inadvertencies cast blemishes upon a great character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat intimate situations as matters of consequence: keep a decent appearance even when alone together to prevent familiarity becoming contemptible. Apologising after being seen in deshabille may be poorly received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain, simple exordium and conformity to classical models
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening lines of an epic (Milton's example) are praised as 'plain, simple and unadorned' and as conforming to the example of Homer and the precept of Horace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good invocation/exordium should be clear and unornamented, fitting the gravity and source of the subject (e.g., invoking the Muse/Holy Spirit when treating creation). Simplicity and classical conformity are virtues in opening a great poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive, striking imaginative incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Original, powerful images and incidents (e.g., 'The Nine Days Astonishment' of the fallen angels; division of Hell into seas of fire and firm ground; exclusion of Hope) are instances of great and fruitful invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value scenes and conceptions that are both surprising and capacious — imaginative particulars that enlarge the reader's view of the subject and stick in the mind as memorable inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex, interwoven characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective heroic/antagonist speeches assemble multiple passions (pride, envy, revenge, obstinacy, despair, impenitence) into a compounded portrayal (Milton's Satan praised for this).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterization benefits from speeches and descriptions that entwine several motives and passions, revealing a rounded, psychologically plausible actor whose utterances both unify and distribute those traits across the work to 'raise and terrifie the Reader's Imagination.'
